balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For General Mills: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For General Mills: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For General Mills: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For General Mills: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For General Mills: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For General Mills: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For General Mills: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For General Mills: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For General Mills: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Segment net sales
segmentRevenue.content:
General Mills reports four segments: North America Retail (branded cereal, snacks, baking and meals sold through US/Canada retail -- roughly 55-60% of sales), Pet (Blue Buffalo), North America Foodservice and International.

For General Mills: NA Retail has been shrinking every year since FY2023 (volume-led) while Pet and NA Foodservice have grown -- the mix shift is diluting the margin profile, since NA Retail is the highest-margin segment by a wide margin.

What to watch:

  • Whether NA Retail's decline is stabilising or still accelerating
  • Pet's growth rate versus the category (competition from Mars/Nestle Purina)
  • International's small, volatile base -- currency and single-market swings dominate it

segmentProfit.title: Segment operating profit
segmentProfit.content:
Segment operating profit before corporate items, interest and tax -- the profitability of each segment on the sales shown in the chart above. Disclosed annually only; the quarterly filings give segment net sales but not segment profit.

For General Mills: NA Retail supplies the large majority of consolidated operating profit, so a margin squeeze there (commodity cost, trade spend, elasticity-driven volume loss) moves the whole company's earnings far more than an equivalent move in Pet or Foodservice.

What to watch:

  • NA Retail margin trend versus its sales decline -- is profit falling faster or slower than sales
  • Pet segment profit after the Blue Buffalo step-up in marketing/promotion spend
  • Whether International ever becomes profit-material or stays a rounding error

organicGrowth.title: Organic growth: volume vs price/mix
organicGrowth.content:
Organic net sales growth excludes the effect of acquisitions, divestitures, foreign exchange and the 53rd week, and is decomposed into volume (units sold) and price/mix (list price increases, promotion/trade spend, and shift between higher- and lower-priced products).

For General Mills: both contributions have been negative or flat in most recent periods -- volume has been the larger drag as price increases taken in FY2023-2024 pushed value-conscious consumers toward private label, and the FY2026 price/mix line turning negative shows the company now giving some of that pricing back (increased promotion) to defend volume.

What to watch:

  • Whether volume stabilises (the bull case) or price/mix turns more negative to chase it (margin risk)
  • Total organic growth versus the segment-level organic growth lines in the KPI table -- is the drag concentrated in NA Retail or broad-based
  • Organic growth versus reported revenue growth -- the gap is FX, portfolio and the 53rd week

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For General Mills: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
